title: Huawei's Ascend chose the hardest road: not compatible with Nvidia
dek: For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that does not solve a chokehold problem but instead goes into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets more exhausting the longer you do it.
why: The first half is about how the book was written, with low information density; from the two key decisions at Ascend's founding, Fang Xingdong gives a lot of first-hand detail and judgment that only appears in the book.
who: Founders, investors and engineers watching domestic compute, the semiconductor supply chain and AI infrastructure, especially those who want to understand the difference between Ascend's and Nvidia's routes.
skip: The first ~13 minutes cover the origins of six books and the interview process, with little bearing on investment judgment.

points.h: Ascend's harshest decision was not being compatible with Nvidia
points.body: At Ascend's founding there were two choices. The first was whether AI chips should be specialized or general-purpose; Liao Heng, as chief scientist, judged that AI should be a general-purpose product, and the architecture choice has been proven right today. The second was harder: whether to be compatible with Nvidia. Many domestic chips chose compatibility, with the benefit that Nvidia's existing ecosystem and tools could all be shared. But Xu Zhijun was firm from the start that they must take a different path. Fang Xingdong believes this choice was extremely bold at the time, and that many times along the way they faced enormous challenges — because the entire Chinese IT industry has been a follower industry for three or four decades, and had never developed based on its own root technologies.

points.h: Anything you do as a follower gets more exhausting the longer you do it
points.body: Fang Xingdong recalls having dinner with Xu Zhijun three years ago, when Xu Zhijun said, half to himself: Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets more exhausting the longer you do it. There are two kinds of following: in standardized products, Chinese companies can always catch up and even overtake, but by the time they overtake, there is no profit left in the industry — 2G to 5G, PCs, phones all went this way; in non-standardized areas, such as competing with Cisco in routers for so many years, they have not drawn closer. In Xu Zhijun's eyes, what Huawei did in the past was also following. So Ascend is special among the six products: the other five solve chokehold problems and address survival first, while Ascend was not choked in 2019 — it is a fully proactive compute product.

points.h: With process choked off, only system innovation can make it back
points.body: Each generation of industry chips gains roughly 20% or more in performance, mainly from the increase in transistor count driven by advanced process improvements. Huawei lost this premise and can only gain performance through system innovation and breakthroughs — stacked compute, interconnect, higher integration. Fang Xingdong explains with a car metaphor: before, you just had to make the engine stronger and stronger; now the engine is constrained and cannot be enlarged, so you can only make the car run well through architecture, weight reduction, heat dissipation and other factors. Nvidia's solution is to keep working on the engine, because TSMC can still manufacture it. In the interview Liao Heng uses the metaphor of an 18-story pagoda: many companies are good at only one layer because of the great division of labor, while Huawei is forced to do manufacturing, ecosystem and chip design all at once.

points.h: Huawei has to pull the domestic supply chain up with it
points.body: Previously Huawei did design, relied on the global supply chain, had TSMC manufacture, could choose the best international partners for other components, directly buy American products and assemble them, sell at a good price with a brand premium, and profits were decent. Now it cannot cooperate abroad, TSMC cannot process for it, and domestic processes are still lacking in every respect, so Huawei has no choice but to support and drive the domestic supply chain — only then does it have a way to survive and get products manufactured. So the challenge of the past seven years is not just improving its own capabilities, but also driving the entire supply chain — without driving it, independent autonomy is impossible. Manufacturing is not Huawei's main business, but it has to help companies like SMIC and Yangtze Memory keep advancing process, yield and quality.

points.h: Ascend's significance is not that Huawei survived, but that the industry has an engine
points.body: In the past, Huawei's product launches and iterations were still based on American root technologies and the industrial ecosystem, and the high-value components of a phone were basically foreign. Now Huawei's phones, including Ascend, almost 100% drive the domestic supply chain. Fang Xingdong believes the greatest significance of the Tao Law is not that Huawei itself can survive and be autonomous, but that China's entire semiconductor industry and entire IT industry have their own engine, which never existed before. Huawei's rapid development represents the rapid development of the entire industrial ecosystem. He also points out that the market, looking at reports, news or public opinion, has not yet realized that we are at this inflection point in the cycle — mention Nvidia and people think it is formidable, mention Huawei and they say it is policy that makes everyone use it.

points.h: It is not a question of difficulty, but of cognition and resolve
points.body: Fang Xingdong believes doing communications versus doing IT is essentially not a question of difficulty but of cognition and resolve — whether you dare to do it. The most typical example is the Gauss database: among these six products Ascend stood out, and the least conspicuous may be Gauss, but the database is a half-century-old industry with a relatively stable market, and if it really gets choked it is deadly. Huawei at the time wanted to acquire or support domestic vendors, but after research found none of them were up to it; domestic companies could only grow in the cracks of American giants, with small scale, weak R&D capability and weak product innovation. So Huawei decided to do it itself, benchmarking Oracle, and from 2011 and 2012 invested 1 billion, 2 billion, 3 billion yuan a year, without knowing whether there would be any output in the future.

points.h: The future is two centers, not one replacing the other
points.body: Fang Xingdong judges that global high tech moving from a single system centered on the US to two centers is the general trend; politics will not allow a continued single center — the US will not allow it, and China will not allow it either. He believes a single center is itself abnormal, and only two centers can create competition — only with two systems does every consumer, every company, every country, no matter how big or small, have a choice, and not be choked into a forced either-or. So the mission of Huawei's six products is to go from being the second choice to being the better choice; it is not a simple substitution relationship with Nvidia, but each has its strengths, they complement each other, and they compete and cooperate. He admits the American system is currently stronger, with its advantage mainly in advanced manufacturing, and that Huawei, under process constraints, relies on the Tao Law not to be left behind; once advanced process is also broken through, it can work both ways at once.

points.h: The tech war won in the short term, at a greater long-term cost
points.body: Fang Xingdong believes the US did indeed suppress Huawei through the tech war, but cannot solve the problem in the long term. He reasons: without the national confrontation of 2017 and 2018, Huawei might have been at least one-third of Nvidia and one-third of Apple, possibly China's largest company by market cap; in 2019 Huawei had already surpassed Apple, and its global shipments briefly surpassed Samsung for one quarter. Nvidia today is dominant alone; if it had from the start advanced side by side with Huawei in AI chips, it could not have reached today's position. He judges that once the side being attacked builds a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, and the other side cannot eliminate it even under the harshest conditions, it will be even harder to eliminate later; it will only grow stronger, turning from one monopoly into two competitors.

quotes.text: He said Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets more exhausting the longer you do it.
I have been in this industry for 30 years, and I feel that many of my past understandings can all be reset to zero.
Without the tech war, Huawei is an excellent company, but it might not, would not become a great company; but with the tech war, it will certainly become a great company.

So the hurdles Huawei currently faces are, with technology, actually about driving the improvement of all of China's industry, the entire supply chain, but many things it has to do itself first, because if it does not do them, no one else can.
Once the side being attacked, whether Huawei or China, builds a self-cycle, a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, frankly speaking it becomes a long-term competitor.
